prediction:
1) Anovulatory dysfunctional uterine bleeding (AUB-O) — Most likely given negative pregnancy test, normal pelvic ultrasound and normal endometrial sampling; common cause across reproductive and perimenopausal ages. Recommend clinical review of cycle pattern and measurement of serum FSH/LH/prolactin and TSH if age/cycle history suggests anovulation.

2) Endometrial polyp — Can cause irregular bleeding and may be missed on TVUS or focal curettage. If bleeding persists, diagnostic hysteroscopy (with directed removal) is the next step.

3) Cervical pathology (cervicitis, cervical polyp, dysplasia/cancer) — Normal endometrial sampling does not exclude a cervical source. Recommend urgent speculum exam with cervical inspection, cervical cytology (Pap) and high-risk HPV testing; obtain cervical cultures if discharge/infection suspected.

4) Coagulation disorder (e.g., von Willebrand disease, platelet dysfunction, anticoagulant effect) — Especially if bleeding is heavy or there is personal/family history of bleeding. Obtain CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, platelet count and consider von Willebrand panel and review for anticoagulant use.

5) Iatrogenic/hormonal causes (exogenous hormones, intrauterine device-related bleeding, recent stop/start of HRT or OCPs, NSAID/anticoagulant use) — Medication/device history can explain abnormal bleeding; perform a focused medication and device review and consider stopping/switching offending agents if identified.

If you want, I can request any of the specific tests/examinations above (speculum exam/Pap/HPV, CBC/coagulation studies, hormonal labs, hysteroscopy) — tell me which single test or exam to order first.
